description: The Core is a driven team that turns hard science into tools that matter. We're building an SI-powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets NASA's microgravity combustion data to deliver fire safety insights for Moon and Mars crews. I bring a physics olympiad background, an engineer's mindset and hands-on experience building real systems with CAD and code. We want teammates who are serious about shipping, a Python/data or ML developer and a frontend/UI developer.
summary:
Freefall Fire Atlas is a fire safety dashboard for spacecraft, stations, lunar and Martian bases and pressurized rovers, built on the NASA PSI combustion investigations. For each habitat it answers one question. When a fire starts, what should the crew do, and how certain can that answer be?

This matters because exploration habitats will breathe air never tested for solid fires in space. On the Moon, at 34% oxygen and 8.2 psia, stopping the fans no longer starves a flame.

We ranked all 23 PSI investigations for each habitat, built a system-dynamics fire model with our own model of the oxygen limit, calibrated it against eight NASA observations and simulated 1,920 fires per habitat and crew response. Stopping the fans controls 92% of fires on the station and none in a Moon base. Smoke warns before heat everywhere, and our neural network, trained on ISS flight data, matches the station detector on runs it never saw.

The dashboard exports its data and model for other modelers and runs locally in the browser.
details:
What it does. For five habitats, a Moon base, a pressurized rover, a Mars base, a spacecraft in transit and a space station, the dashboard gives a fire safety assessment. It shows which crew response works and how often, how large the fire grows, when each detector alarms, and which unknown would change the answer most. Every result carries its range across 120 calibrated model versions. A custom scenario page runs all of them on any oxygen, pressure, gravity, volume, airflow, material, crew timing and agent reach.

How it works.

1. Evidence. We read all 23 PSI combustion investigations and 38 findings from NASA technical reports and ordered their objectives, fuels, sample sizes, oxygen, pressure, airflow, variables and sensors. 103 numbers were checked against the PSI metadata.

2. Fire model. A system-dynamics model with stocks of fuel, burning area, cabin oxygen, smoke, carbon monoxide and heat. A flame survives only above an oxygen limit that depends on airflow and gravity, O2 limit = a0 + a1/(u+c) + b·u, with u = sqrt(fan² + (ub·sqrt(g))²).

3. Calibration. Approximate Bayesian computation over 60,000 parameter draws. We keep the 138 that reproduce eight NASA observations from ACME BRE, BASS, SoFIE, Saffire and FM2 studies.

4. Simulation. A Monte Carlo of 1,920 fires per habitat and response, with material, crew reaction time and the share of agent reaching the flame drawn at random.

5. Detection. A neural network written from scratch, trained on SAME-R ISS flight sensor data and tested on runs it never saw. It reached 91.2% balanced accuracy, against 91.8% for the station's light-scattering channel alone.

Results. Stopping the fans controls 92% of fires on the station and none in a Moon base. Adding CO₂ raises the Moon-base figure to 55%, between 19 and 81% across model versions. Smoke detectors alarm before heat detectors in every habitat, and an alarm 30 seconds earlier cuts the smoke a crew breathes by 36% in a Mars base and 34% on the station.

Benefits. Designers and mission planners see in one place which evidence applies to their habitat and where it is missing. Modelers receive structured data and a calibrated flammability model. Equipment developers see how much early detection is worth. The same evidence serves sealed spaces on Earth, such as submarine compartments and mine refuge chambers.

Tools. JavaScript, HTML and SVG in a single file that works offline. Python and Node.js for data extraction and testing.
